grades.quote: When the hart is running in user-mode, the value in SIE is ignored, and supervisor-level interrupts are enabled.
grades.reason: RISC-V sstatus description. It shows a few user vs. supervisor differences: SPP records the prior privilege level, and SIE is ignored in user mode. It does not give a general comparison or say what the levels are for.

grades.quote: HS-mode is more privileged than VS-mode, and VS-mode is more privileged than VU-mode.
grades.reason: Lists RISC-V privilege modes (U, VU, HS, VS, M) with their nominal privilege and ordering. It says little about how user execution differs from privileged execution or what the levels are for.

grades.quote: When SUM=0, S-mode memory accesses to pages that are accessible by U-mode (U=1 in Figure 67) will fault. When SUM=1, these accesses are permitted.
grades.reason: Gives one concrete difference between S-mode and U-mode: S-mode accesses to user pages fault unless SUM is set. It also says S-mode can never execute user pages and explains why SUM protects user memory. This is a narrow aspect of the user vs. privileged distinction.

grades.quote: the code running in user mode
grades.reason: It sits in a section on the two processor modes but is about user-level threads (fibers) that avoid mode switches. It only touches user mode vs. kernel execution and does not explain the difference or purpose of the privilege levels.
